content: 1. Clinical evaluation of household and close contacts for tuberculosis (TB) should be based on their risk of having or developing TB disease or the potential consequences if the disease develops. Priority should be given to contacts who are children with symptoms suggestive of TB, children under 5 years of age, children with known or suspected immunocompromising conditions (especially those living with HIV), and child contacts of index cases with multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 2. Contact investigation is recommended for household and close contacts when the index case has any of the following characteristics: sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB, MDR or XDR TB (proven or suspected), is a person living with HIV, or is a child under 5 years of age. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 3. Contact investigation may also be conducted for household and close contacts of all other index cases with pulmonary TB, in addition to those covered in the previous recommendation. (Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 4. Children under 5 years of age who are household or close contacts of people with TB and who, after appropriate clinical evaluation, are found not to have TB disease should be given 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at a dose of 10 mg/kg per day (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day). (Strong recommendation, high quality of evidence) 5. Children under 5 years of age who are household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and who are found not to have TB disease on clinical evaluation or according to national guidelines should receive TB preventive treatment, even if TB infection testing is unavailable. (Strong recommendation, high certainty in the estimates of effect) 6. Children aged 5 years and older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of people with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and who are found not to have TB disease by clinical evaluation or according to national guidelines may be given TB preventive treatment. (Conditional recommendation, low certainty in the estimates of effect) 7. Recommended options for TB infection treatment, regardless of HIV status, include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. (Strong recommendation, moderate to high certainty in the estimates of effect) 8. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive TB infection test and are unlikely to have TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily IPT. This should be given regardless of whether the person is on antiretroviral therapy (ART), the degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. (Conditional recommendation, low certainty in the estimates of effect) 9. In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of people with TB should be counseled and tested for HIV. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 10. In settings with low HIV prevalence, all household members and close contacts of people with TB who have symptoms compatible with TB disease may be offered counseling and testing for HIV as part of their clinical evaluation. (Conditional recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 11. All household contacts of an index case who is a person living with HIV should be counseled and tested for HIV. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 12. Children living with HIV who are more than 12 months of age, unlikely to have TB disease based on symptom-based screening, and have no contact with a TB case should be offered 6 months of IPT (10 mg/kg per day, range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day) as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services if living in settings with high TB prevalence. (Strong recommendation, low quality of evidence) 13. Children living with HIV in settings with medium or low TB prevalence might also be offered 6 months of IPT as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care services. (Conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence) 14. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease should receive TB preventive treatment as part of a comprehensive package of HIV care. This includes those on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or availability of TB infection testing. (Strong recommendation, high certainty in the estimates of effect) 15. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who are in contact with a person with TB and unlikely to have TB disease based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should receive TB preventive treatment. (Strong recommendation, moderate certainty in the estimates of effect) 16. Children aged 12 months and older living with HIV who are unlikely to have TB disease based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of a comprehensive package of HIV prevention and care if they live in a setting with high TB transmission, regardless of contact with TB. (Strong recommendation, low certainty in the estimates of effect) 17. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may receive TB preventive treatment. (Conditional recommendation, low certainty in the estimates of effect) 18. Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous peripheral lymphadenitis living in settings with high HIV prevalence (or with confirmed HIV infection) should not be treated with intermittent regimens (e.g., twice-weekly or thrice-weekly doses). (Strong recommendation, low-to-moderate quality evidence against intermittent treatment in children) 19. In all patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, thrice-weekly dosing is not recommended during either the intensive or continuation phases of therapy. Daily dosing remains the recommended frequency. (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty in the evidence) 20. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by multidrug-resistant bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone within a well-functioning MDR-TB control program and an appropriate MDR-TB regimen. The decision to treat should be made by a clinician experienced in managing pediatric TB. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence) 21. In children with MDR/RR-TB aged below 6 years, an all-oral treatment regimen containing bedaquiline may be used. (New conditional recommendation, very low certainty of the evidence) 22. A shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months is recommended for eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines used in this regimen for more than 1 month and in whom resistance to fluoroquinolones has been excluded. (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty in the evidence) 23. Bedaquiline should be included in longer MDR-TB regimens for patients aged 18 years or more. It may also be included in longer MDR-TB regimens for patients aged 6–17 years. (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty in the estimates of effect) 24. In children with MDR/RR-TB aged below 3 years, delamanid may be used as part of longer regimens. (New conditional recommendation, very low certainty of the evidence) 25. In MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens, all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent should be included to ensure treatment starts with at least four TB agents likely to be effective, and at least three agents are included for the rest of treatment if bedaquiline is stopped. If only one or two Group A agents are used, both Group B agents should be included. If the regimen cannot be composed with agents from Groups A and B alone, Group C agents are added to complete it. (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty in the estimates of effect) 26. All children treated for TB should be recorded and reported by the National Tuberculosis Program (NTP) in one of two age bands: 0–4 years and 5–14 years. This recommendation is based on good clinical practice and will be incorporated into the operational handbook with revised age bands for reporting. The updated age bands for reporting TB in children and adolescents are now: 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, and 15–19 years. 27. In children with presumptive pulmonary TB attending healthcare facilities, integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB. (New interim conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence)
